name: Unlawful possession of firearm (after felony conviction and before the five-year release anniversary)
officialTitle: UNLAWFUL POSSESSION OF FIREARM.
conduct: Intentionally, knowingly or recklessly possessing a firearm in the specified felony circumstance. After a qualifying felony conviction and before the fifth anniversary of release from confinement following that conviction or release from community supervision, parole or mandatory supervision, whichever date is later. The clock is not simply five years after conviction, and residence possession is not exempt during this window. The predicate must qualify under §46.04(f), subject to (g): the statute’s designation, elements and penitentiary-punishment tests cannot be replaced by a colloquial felony label, and its exception looks to Texas felony designation/elements at the time of firearm possession. Possession requires actual care, custody, control or management and the applicable culpable mental state. Under §6.01(b), possession is voluntary if the person knowingly obtains or receives the thing or is aware of control long enough to terminate it; mere proximity is not automatically possession. The Chapter 46 firearm definition and its narrow antique/replica exclusion apply. These choices describe the Texas offense only; they do not restore firearm rights or resolve separate federal restrictions or individual constitutional challenges.
penalty: Third-degree felony: ordinarily two to ten years in prison and a possible fine up to $10,000. Section 46.11 can increase punishment by one offense category when its knowledge and school-zone/function findings are proved beyond a reasonable doubt; this ordinary choice does not assume those findings. Qualifying prior convictions and case-specific findings can change punishment.

Qualifying prior convictions and case-specific findings can change punishment.

name: Unlawful possession of firearm (criminal street gang member carrying in a vehicle or watercraft)
officialTitle: UNLAWFUL POSSESSION OF FIREARM.
conduct: A person who is a member of a criminal street gang intentionally, knowingly or recklessly carries a handgun on or about the person in a motor vehicle or watercraft. The §71.01(d) gang definition requires three or more persons with a common identifying sign/symbol or identifiable leadership who continuously or regularly associate in criminal activities; association alone is not automatically membership in such a gang. This is the specific handgun-carry branch, not every firearm possessed by someone called a gang member. Possession requires actual care, custody, control or management and the applicable culpable mental state. Under §6.01(b), possession is voluntary if the person knowingly obtains or receives the thing or is aware of control long enough to terminate it; mere proximity is not automatically possession. The Chapter 46 firearm definition and its narrow antique/replica exclusion apply. These choices describe the Texas offense only; they do not restore firearm rights or resolve separate federal restrictions or individual constitutional challenges.
penalty: Class A misdemeanor: ordinarily up to one year in jail, a fine up to $4,000, or both. Section 46.11 can increase punishment by one offense category when its knowledge and school-zone/function findings are proved beyond a reasonable doubt; this ordinary choice does not assume those findings. Qualifying prior convictions and case-specific findings can change punishment.

name: Unlawful possession of firearm (qualifying Class A family/household assault conviction within five-year window)
officialTitle: UNLAWFUL POSSESSION OF FIREARM.
conduct: Intentionally, knowingly or recklessly possessing a firearm after conviction under §22.01 punishable as a Class A misdemeanor and involving a family or household member, before the fifth anniversary of the later release from confinement or community supervision following that misdemeanor. Not every misdemeanor or assault conviction supplies this predicate. Family includes the specified relatives, former spouses, parents of the same child and foster relationships; household includes people living together and membership includes a former household member under §71.006. Possession requires actual care, custody, control or management and the applicable culpable mental state. name: Unlawful possession of metal or body armor by felon (after felony conviction)
officialTitle: UNLAWFUL POSSESSION OF METAL OR BODY ARMOR BY FELON.
conduct: After a felony conviction, intentionally, knowingly or recklessly possessing metal or body armor: a body covering manifestly designed, made or adapted to protect against gunfire. The five-year/residence qualifications in the separate firearm statute are not silently imported into this armor statute. Voluntary possession and actual control must be established; merely being near an item is not enough. This choice does not decide separate federal restrictions or case-specific constitutional challenges.
penalty: Third-degree felony: ordinarily two to ten years in prison and a possible fine up to $10,000. Qualifying prior convictions and case-specific findings can change punishment.

name: Deadly weapon in penal institution (carrying, possessing or concealing while confined)
officialTitle: DEADLY WEAPON IN PENAL INSTITUTION.
conduct: While confined in a penal institution, intentionally, knowingly or recklessly carrying a deadly weapon on or about the person, or possessing or concealing one in the institution. Penal institution has the §1.07(a)(37) meaning of a lawfully designated place for confinement after arrest, charge or conviction; a civil commitment facility is not automatically substituted. Deadly weapon includes a firearm and the other designed/adapted or manner-of-use lethal-capability alternatives in §1.07(a)(17). Section 46.10(b) supplies an affirmative defense when the conduct was authorized by an institutional employee. Its rule allowing prosecution under this or another applicable Chapter 46 section is not treated as automatic cumulative punishment.
penalty: Third-degree felony: ordinarily two to ten years in prison and a possible fine up to $10,000. Section 46.11 can increase punishment by one offense category when its knowledge and school-zone/function findings are proved beyond a reasonable doubt; this ordinary choice does not assume those findings. Qualifying prior convictions and case-specific findings can change punishment.

name: Prohibited substances and items in correctional or civil commitment facility (providing substances or possessing with intent to provide; ordinary)
officialTitle: PROHIBITED SUBSTANCES AND ITEMS IN CORRECTIONAL OR CIVIL COMMITMENT FACILITY.
conduct: Providing, or possessing with intent to provide, an alcoholic beverage, controlled substance or dangerous drug to someone in correctional custody or residing in a civil commitment facility, except on a practitioner’s prescription. The prescription language here is the (a)(1) exception, not a general phone/weapon authorization. This ordinary grade excludes the correctional-facility employee enhancements; civil-facility employment is not automatically correctional-facility employment. Correctional facility is limited by §38.11(f)(6) to the specified municipal/county jail, TDCJ confinement and TDCJ contract-designated places, plus Family Code secure correctional/detention facilities; the broader general definition is not substituted wholesale. Civil commitment facility has the §1.07(a)(8-a) meaning tied to Chapter 841 civil commitment. Expressly required intent must be established. Section 6.01 governs voluntary conduct and possession, and §6.02 supplies general culpability rules where an offense does not state a mental state. The applicable mental-state instructions require case-specific review; this summary does not declare accidental presence of an item automatic guilt.
penalty: Third-degree felony: ordinarily two to ten years in prison and a possible fine up to $10,000. The completed offense is described here; subsection (h) separately makes qualifying attempts under (a), (b) or (c) third-degree felonies rather than applying the ordinary one-category reduction. Qualifying prior convictions and case-specific findings can change punishment.

Civil commitment facility has the §1.07(a)(8-a) meaning tied to Chapter 841 civil commitment. Expressly required intent must be established. Section 6.01 governs voluntary conduct and possession, and §6.02 supplies general culpability rules where an offense does not state a mental state. The applicable mental-state instructions require case-specific review; this summary does not declare accidental presence of an item automatic guilt. The correctional-employee enhancements in (g-1)/(g-2) apply only to (a)(1), (b) or (c), not automatically to this branch.
penalty: Third-degree felony: ordinarily two to ten years in prison and a possible fine up to $10,000. Qualifying prior convictions and case-specific findings can change punishment.
